strengths: The paper addresses a critical and highly relevant problem in text-to-image (T2I) generation: why and how models succeed or fail at generating specified spatial relations between objects.

The mechanistic interpretability approach is rigorous and thorough. The authors do not merely correlate attention maps with output; they provide direct causal evidence through head-ablation, value-output (VO) injection/patching, and representation manipulation (vector arithmetic on T5 embeddings).

The discovery of two completely different circuit mechanisms depending on the text encoder (RTE's modular two-stage circuit vs. T5's compact information-fusion circuit) is highly insightful. This cleanly bridges the literature debate on whether spatial reasoning failures originate from the text encoder or the diffusion backbone.

The proposed 'Attention Synopsis' paradigm offers a systematic, scalable way to digest and summarize millions of cross-attention patterns over multiple denoising steps, which can serve as a valuable tool for future interpretability research in diffusion models.

The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, clearly illustrated, and includes comprehensive details in the appendix (including dataset generation logic and variance partitioning mathematics) to ensure reproducibility.
weaknesses: The experiments are conducted on a highly simplified, synthetic dataset (3 shapes, 2 colors, 8 relations, gray background). While toy setups are standard and necessary for clean mechanistic interpretability, there is a large domain gap to real-world, large-scale T2I models. A brief discussion on how these localized circuits might map or scale to fully trained commercial DiTs would strengthen the paper.

The observed high sensitivity of the T5-DiT model to minor prompt perturbations (e.g., adding 'the') might be primarily driven by the fact that the DiT is trained from scratch on highly templated text data. Pretrained T5 embeddings are robust, but a DiT trained on a narrow template space likely overfits to the exact embedding directions of those templates. Clarifying this distinction (pretrained encoder vs. scratch-trained DiT mapping) would improve the robustness discussion.

strengths: The paper applies rigorous mechanistic interpretability techniques (such as circuit finding, attention synopses, and causal interventions) to Diffusion Transformers (DiTs), which is highly novel and timely given that most mechanistic interpretability works focus primarily on autoregressive language models.
The contrast between how the model processes spatial relations under different text encoders (RTE vs. pretrained T5) is clear, illuminating, and well-substantiated by the experiments.

The paper provides strong causal evidence to support its claims, particularly through head-specific ablation/injection and vector arithmetic on the T5 embedding space to systematically manipulate the generated spatial layout.
The methodology is exceptionally detailed, with clear mathematical formulations for variance partitioning and attention map synopses in the appendix.
weaknesses: The study is conducted entirely on a highly simplified, synthetic toy dataset with basic shapes and solid colors at 128x128 resolution. It remains an open question how cleanly these specific localized circuits generalize to complex, large-scale open-domain models trained on natural images and captions.

The performance collapse of the T5-DiT under slight prompt perturbations (e.g., adding 'the') may be a consequence of overfitting the DiT to the highly rigid template format of the synthetic training set, rather than an inherent limitation of T5's contextual embeddings in general-purpose models. This distinction should be discussed more carefully.

strengths: Presents a novel and thorough mechanistic interpretability study on how Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) generate spatial relations, an important and timely topic in generative modeling.
Introduces 'Attention Synopsis', a scalable and practical framework to aggregate and analyze millions of attention maps across layers, heads, and diffusion steps.

Provides a clear and fascinating comparison between models using random token embeddings (RTE) and contextual pretrained embeddings (T5), showing how the text encoder fundamentally alters the downstream neural circuits.
Validates the identified circuit components with rigorous causal interventions, including head-specific ablations, representation injection, and targeted vector arithmetic in the embedding space.

Exposes a key vulnerability of contextual text encoders: although T5-based DiTs are highly expressive, their tendency to fuse spatial relations into object tokens makes them sensitive to minor out-of-domain prompt variations (such as adding 'the').
weaknesses: The analysis is constrained to a highly simplified, synthetic 2D toy dataset with basic geometric shapes (circles, triangles, squares) and simple spatial relations. It remains unclear how cleanly these distinct circuits generalize to complex, open-vocabulary, real-world scenes.

The scope of architectures tested is limited mostly to PixArt-style DiT backbones. Exploring other popular designs, such as MM-DiT (which uses joint attention) or standard U-Net-based diffusion models, would strengthen the generalizability of the findings.

The representation analysis of T5 contextual embeddings relies heavily on a linear factorization assumption. Although variance partitioning and vector arithmetic show compelling results, T5-XXL's multi-layered self-attention can introduce complex, non-linear contextual dependencies that are not fully captured by this linear model.

strengths: Excellent formulation of mechanistic interpretability on Diffusion Transformers (DiTs). It addresses a highly critical problem in text-to-image models (spatial relation compositionality) from a fundamental, circuit-level perspective.

The paper successfully bridges and unifies two main schools of thought in the literature: whether spatial reasoning fails due to cross-attention issues or poor text encoder representations, showing that different text encoders trigger completely different internal circuit mechanisms.

Clean and elegant methods for identifying circuits: 'Attention Synopsis' to reduce the complex cross-attention tensor, and 'Weight-space head screening', which allows identifying heads purely from weights and positional embeddings without expensive generation/evaluation loops.

Robust causal validation: The authors don't just find correlations in attention maps; they validate them using causal interventions (attention ablation, injecting VO outputs of the relation head into the object head, and vector arithmetic in the T5 embedding space).
Strong generalization of the methods to CLIP-DiT and larger pre-trained models like PixArt-Sigma, demonstrating the broad utility of the proposed diagnostic tools.
weaknesses: The study is mainly conducted in a highly simplified synthetic setting (128x128 images, simple 2D shapes, 8 relations). Although synthetic setups are standard and necessary for clean mechanistic interpretability, this limits the direct applicability of the findings to more complex real-world prompts where relations might not be so cleanly factorized.

While the brittleness of T5-DiT to simple prompt perturbations (like adding 'the') is convincingly shown and explained, the paper does not explore potential training or architectural remedies to make the contextual fusion more robust.
A few minor typos and writing inconsistencies exist (e.g., 'then they the correct binding' on page 3, 'andspatial' on page 3, 'casual manipulation' in Section 4.4, and the missing link in Section C).

strengths: Provides deep and compelling mechanistic insights into how Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) generate spatial relationships, revealing two fundamentally different circuit behaviors (modular vs. information-fused) depending on the choice of text encoder (RTE vs. T5/CLIP).

Goes beyond correlation to establish causation using rigorous interpretability techniques, including activation patching (injecting the VO output of L2H8 into L4H3) and targeted representation editing via vector arithmetic in the T5 embedding space.

Mechanistically explains a well-known real-world issue: the brittleness of pretrained text-to-image models to minor prompt perturbations (e.g., adding filler words like 'the'), showing how context shifts in the text representation distort downstream spatial gradients.

Proposes a highly efficient, weight-space screening method for identifying spatial relation heads directly from static weights and positional embeddings, avoiding expensive image generation during search and demonstrating scalability.
weaknesses: The primary analysis is conducted on a highly simplified, synthetic dataset of basic geometric shapes and solid colors. While appropriate for controlled mechanistic interpretability, the complexity of real-world scenes is significantly higher.

The localization of the object generation circuit is less clean than the spatial relation circuit; ablating the primary object generation head (L4H3) only drops shape accuracy from 90% to 76%, indicating that object feature routing is still somewhat distributed across other heads or layers.
Some figures and tables are placed quite far from their initial text references (e.g., Figure 8 is mentioned on page 1 but located on page 11), which slightly disrupts the reading flow.

strengths: Extends mechanistic interpretability concepts (usually restricted to autoregressive LLMs) to Diffusion Transformers (DiTs), offering a novel perspective on how text-to-image models process spatial relations.

Goes beyond simple correlation analysis of attention maps by using causal interventions, such as injecting the activation of the spatial relation head into positional embeddings, and targeted head ablations to verify functional circuits.

Provides valuable insights into the differences between contextual (T5/CLIP) and non-contextual (RTE) text encoders, demonstrating that T5 fuses spatial attributes directly into object representation tokens, which leads to generalization brittleness when perturbed.

Formulates a mathematically rigorous weight-space screening method based on QK interactions and variance partitioning, allowing the identification of relation heads without expensive image generation loops.
Extremely thorough supplementary material containing detailed mathematical derivations, additional analyses across multiple model scales (mini, micro, nano), and clean pseudocode implementations.
weaknesses: The core findings and clean circuit mappings are heavily reliant on a highly simplified, synthetic dataset of colored shapes on flat gray backgrounds. The complexity of these circuits in models trained on complex, real-world scenes with rich backgrounds and multiple overlapping relationships is not fully explored.

The validation on a real-world pre-trained model (PixArt-Sigma) is limited because, as the authors note, the pre-trained model itself has very poor spatial-relation accuracy (only 8 out of 30 object pairs showed non-trivial accuracy). This makes it difficult to verify if a fully functioning relation circuit behaves the same way in large-scale natural-image diffusion models.

The 'Attention Synopsis' aggregates attention scores over time steps to maintain tractability, which potentially oversimplifies or masks the intricate time-varying dynamics of the iterative denoising process across the diffusion schedule.
The presentation in the main body is somewhat cluttered and relies too heavily on constant navigation to the appendix (which spans 45 pages) for critical figures, tables, and robustness metrics.
